impacts.caseName: Dental Monitoring SAS v. Align Technology, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the Board's precedential decision in Penumbra correctly held that Dynamic Drinkware's written description analysis for establishing a reference patent's prior art date applies only to pre-AIA law and not to prior art determinations under AIA 35 U.S.C. § 102(d)(2).
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the PTAB's final written decision finding claims of the '409 patent (directed to dental arch imaging using deep learning) obvious, and remanded for further consideration. The court addressed the critical question of when a reference patent can rely on the filing date of its provisional application to qualify as prior art under AIA § 102(d)(2). This decision has significant implications for how provisional application filing dates are used to establish prior art status in IPR proceedings under the AIA.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders may benefit from a more rigorous standard for opponents seeking to use provisional application filing dates to establish prior art references, potentially shielding patents from invalidity challenges in IPR proceedings.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies challenging patent validity in IPR proceedings may face greater difficulty relying on reference patents' provisional filing dates as prior art, increasing costs and uncertainty in patent challenges.

impacts.caseName: Teva Pharmaceuticals International GmbH v. Eli Lilly and Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the enablement requirement for method claims directed to treating headache with anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies permits broad genus claims where any member of the claimed genus would be effective for the recited treatment.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit denied en banc rehearing of a panel decision upholding broad method claims for treating headache using anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies. Judge Dyk dissented, arguing the panel's holding undermines enablement standards for method claims, sustains overly broad claims, and is contrary to Supreme Court precedent. The case has major implications for pharmaceutical and biologic patent scope, particularly for method-of-treatment claims covering broad genera of therapeutic compounds.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders in the pharmaceutical and biologics industries benefit from the ability to obtain and enforce broad method-of-treatment claims covering a genus of therapeutic agents, strengthening exclusivity positions.
impacts.negativeImplications: Generic and biosimilar companies face potentially broader patent barriers to market entry, as the decision permits functionally defined genus claims for treatment methods that may be difficult to design around.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether an exclusive license agreement conveyed 'all substantial rights' in the asserted patents, thereby constituting a virtual assignment that entitled the licensee to sue for infringement without joining the patent owner, and whether the licensee had ceased business operations triggering automatic termination of the agreement.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's dismissal, holding that TexasLDPC's exclusive license from Texas A&M University conveyed all substantial rights in the patents, entitling it to sue without joining the university. The court also held that shifting to patent enforcement did not constitute ceasing business operations under the license agreement. This decision clarifies the standing requirements for exclusive licensees and the scope of rights needed to maintain patent infringement suits independently.
impacts.positiveImplications: Exclusive licensees and patent assertion entities benefit from confirmation that a comprehensive exclusive license can constitute a virtual assignment, allowing enforcement without joining the patent owner as a co-plaintiff.
impacts.negativeImplications: Accused infringers lose an important procedural defense—challenging standing based on failure to join the patent owner—when the exclusive license conveys sufficiently broad rights.

impacts.caseName: Versata Software, LLC v. Ford Motor Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in excluding trade secret damages expert testimony and reducing jury-awarded breach of contract damages in a dispute over automotive configuration software.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the trade secret damages judgment and remanded for a new trial, instructing the district court to reconsider two damages models it had previously rejected. The court also reversed the district court's reduction of breach of contract damages and reinstated the jury's original award. The court affirmed the finding of trade secret misappropriation liability against Ford for developing competing software while licensing Versata's technology. This case provides important guidance on trade secret damages methodology and the scope of protection for licensed software.
impacts.positiveImplications: Software developers and licensors benefit from the court's affirmation of trade secret misappropriation liability and reinstatement of the jury's breach of contract damages, reinforcing protections for proprietary technology shared under license agreements.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies that develop competing products after licensing third-party technology face heightened trade secret misappropriation risk, and the remand for reconsideration of previously excluded damages theories may lead to larger damage awards.

impacts.caseName: Constellation Designs, LLC v. LG Electronics Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to non-uniform constellations for digital communications satisfy the patent eligibility requirement of 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court properly denied JMOL of non-infringement and no damages.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the summary judgment of patent eligibility for certain claims while affirming eligibility for others in a case involving communication system patents used in television broadcasting. The court affirmed the denial of JMOL on non-infringement and damages. This case provides significant guidance on the application of the Alice framework to communications technology patents, distinguishing between claims that merely recite abstract mathematical concepts and those tied to specific technological implementations.
impacts.positiveImplications: Technology companies holding patents on specific implementations of mathematical or algorithmic concepts in communications systems benefit from the court's nuanced approach to eligibility that preserves patent protection for applied innovations.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies in the communications and consumer electronics sectors face continued litigation exposure where patents claim specific technological applications of mathematical methods, as some such claims survive § 101 challenges.

impacts.caseName: Range of Motion Products, LLC v. Armaid Company Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the Egyptian Goddess framework for design patent infringement improperly focuses on differences rather than overall similarity, and whether functionality determinations in design patent claim construction present factual questions for the jury.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit denied en banc rehearing in a design patent case, with multiple judges dissenting. The majority concurrence reaffirmed that the Egyptian Goddess ordinary observer test properly requires comparing similarities and differences, and that functionality determinations in design patent claim construction are appropriately handled by the court. Chief Judge Moore's dissent argued that the current framework improperly shifts focus to dissimilarity and allows courts to resolve infringement at summary judgment without adequate consideration of prior art and jury issues.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from the continued framework that permits resolution of design patent infringement at summary judgment and allows courts to filter out functional elements from design patent claims.
impacts.negativeImplications: Design patent holders face continued risk that courts will resolve infringement disputes at summary judgment based on perceived differences, potentially narrowing the effective scope of design patent protection.

impacts.caseName: Satius Holding, LLC v. Samsung Electronics Co., Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the asserted patent claims were invalid for lack of enablement, even though the district court had found them invalid for indefiniteness on different grounds.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's indefiniteness ruling but affirmed the judgment of invalidity on alternative enablement grounds. The court found that claims directed to a communications apparatus with a coupler matching transmitter impedance to the impedance of air were not enabled by the specification. This decision demonstrates the court's willingness to affirm invalidity on grounds not relied upon below and provides guidance on enablement requirements for claims covering physically challenging implementations.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from the Federal Circuit's willingness to affirm invalidity on alternative grounds, providing additional defensive options even when the district court's original reasoning is overturned.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face the risk that claims may be invalidated on enablement grounds raised for the first time on appeal, even if they successfully challenge the district court's original basis for invalidity.

impacts.caseName: T-Mobile US, Inc. v. KAIFI LLC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Circuit has appellate jurisdiction over a contract interpretation dispute arising from a patent litigation settlement agreement, where the dispute concerns the meaning of 'survives the EPR' but does not necessarily require resolution of a substantial patent law question.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit held it lacked subject-matter jurisdiction over a dispute concerning interpretation of a patent litigation settlement agreement and transferred the case to the Fifth Circuit. The dispute concerned whether T-Mobile owed a contingent payment under the settlement when asserted claims were confirmed patentable in ex parte reexamination. The court determined the dispute was fundamentally one of contract interpretation under state law rather than patent law. This decision clarifies jurisdictional boundaries for post-settlement patent disputes.
impacts.positiveImplications: Parties to patent settlements benefit from clarity that contract interpretation disputes will be resolved under state law standards in regional circuits, potentially providing more predictable outcomes than Federal Circuit patent law analysis.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies involved in patent settlement disputes may face additional litigation costs and delay from jurisdictional transfers, and the ruling creates potential for inconsistent treatment of settlement agreement terms across circuits.

impacts.caseName: Epic Tech, LLC v. Pen-Tech Associates, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court provided sufficient analysis in denying motions for Rule 11 sanctions and attorney fees under 35 U.S.C. § 285 where the patent holder pursued infringement claims despite prior § 101 rejections of related patent applications.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated and remanded the district court's denial of sanctions and attorney fees, finding the court's order provided insufficient detail to permit meaningful appellate review. The case involved a patent holder that pursued infringement claims despite the PTO having rejected claims in related applications under § 101 following Alice. This decision signals that courts must provide thorough analysis when denying fee-shifting motions in cases with significant indicia of exceptionality.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from heightened scrutiny of courts' decisions denying fee-shifting motions, potentially deterring frivolous patent assertions where related claims have been rejected on eligibility grounds.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders and their counsel face increased risk of sanctions and fee awards when pursuing infringement claims despite prior PTO rejections of related claims, as courts must now more thoroughly justify denying such motions.

impacts.caseName: VDPP, LLC v. Volkswagen Group of America, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court abused its discretion in dismissing a patent infringement complaint without leave to amend, awarding attorney fees under 35 U.S.C. § 285, and sanctioning plaintiff's counsel under 28 U.S.C. § 1927.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the district court's dismissal without leave to amend, the award of $207,543.60 in attorney fees to Volkswagen under § 285, and sanctions against plaintiff's counsel. The court held that the plaintiff had implicitly agreed not to amend its complaint in exchange for an extension of time and that the proposed amended complaint was futile. This case reinforces the consequences of pursuing weak patent infringement claims and making procedural concessions.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from affirmation that fee-shifting and sanctions are appropriate when plaintiffs pursue meritless patent claims, providing a meaningful deterrent against abusive patent litigation.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders and litigation counsel face significant financial exposure when pursuing infringement claims that are found to be without merit, particularly when procedural missteps compound substantive weaknesses.

impacts.caseName: Exelixis, Inc. v. MSN Laboratories Private Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to crystalline and amorphous forms of cabozantinib (L)-malate salt satisfy the written description requirement of 35 U.S.C. § 112(a), where the specification primarily described crystalline forms.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the district court's finding that claims of the malate salt patents covering cabozantinib formulations had adequate written description. The case involved Hatch-Waxman litigation over patents protecting Cabometyx®, a cancer treatment drug. This decision is commercially significant for pharmaceutical patent protection, as it confirms that specifications describing specific crystalline salt forms can support broader claims encompassing both crystalline and amorphous forms of the same salt.
impacts.positiveImplications: Brand pharmaceutical companies benefit from broader patent protection for drug substance forms, as specifications describing specific crystalline polymorphs can support claims to the broader genus including amorphous forms, extending exclusivity periods.
impacts.negativeImplications: Generic pharmaceutical companies face stronger patent barriers to market entry, as broader written description support for salt form claims narrows pathways for Paragraph IV certifications and ANDA filings.

impacts.caseName: Archroma U.S., Inc. v. Department of Commerce
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether Commerce's regulation imposing a 15-day deadline for domestic interested parties to indicate intent to participate in sunset reviews of antidumping duty orders conflicts with the governing statute, which is silent on timing.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the Court of International Trade, holding that Commerce's 15-day regulatory deadline for domestic interested parties to express willingness to participate in sunset reviews of antidumping duty orders is a permissible exercise of agency authority. The statute is silent on timing, and the regulation was the product of reasoned decisionmaking within Commerce's delegated power. This decision preserves the procedural framework governing the continuation or revocation of antidumping duties, which directly affects import competition and pricing.
impacts.positiveImplications: Domestic manufacturers and producers benefit from the preservation of Commerce's regulatory framework that ensures orderly administration of sunset reviews, protecting established antidumping duty orders from revocation due to procedural lapses.
impacts.negativeImplications: Foreign exporters and U.S. importers face continued risk that antidumping duties will be maintained through sunset reviews governed by tight regulatory deadlines, even where the statute itself imposes no explicit participation deadline.
